simple: the wires that say where a value should go or come from.
analogy: the room-and-shelf label on a trolley.
precise: the group of signals that carries the address of a transfer; with n address lines, 2n distinct addresses can be named.
source: D1, W1 of F1-40 (pending verification; D1 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the wires that carry the value itself.
analogy: the trolley's load.
precise: the group of signals that carries the data of a transfer; its width (for example 8, 32 or 64 bits) is how many bits move in one transfer.
source: D1 of F1-40 (pending verification; D1 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the extra wires that say what kind of transfer this is and when it is valid.
analogy: the "deliver" or "collect" stamp on the trolley, and the bell that says "now".
precise: signals such as read/write, a clock or strobe that marks valid data, and handshake or error signals; the exact set belongs to each bus's specification.
source: D2 of F1-40 (pending verification; D2 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the circuit that checks an address and wakes up the one device it belongs to.
analogy: the doorkeeper who reads the label.
precise: combinational logic that compares (part of) the address with each device's window and asserts that device's select (chip-select) signal.
source: D1 of F1-40 (pending verification; D1 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the table that says which address range belongs to which device.
analogy: the building's floor plan with room numbers.
precise: the assignment of address ranges (windows) to memories and device registers in an address space; addresses outside every window are holes.
source: D1 of F1-40 (pending verification; D1 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a master is a part that may start transfers; arbitration decides which master goes next.
analogy: Amara deciding which trolley enters the corridor first.
precise: a bus master (in newer documents: an initiator or requester) drives addresses and starts transactions; an arbiter grants the bus to one requesting master at a time by a policy such as fixed priority or round-robin.
source: D2 of F1-40 (pending verification; D2 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: two senders talking on the same wires at once.
analogy: two doors answering the same label.
precise: two drivers enabled on the same line at the same time; with push-pull outputs it can damage parts, with open-drain lines the result is the AND of the senders; either way the value is wrong.
source: D1 of F1-40 (pending verification; D1 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how many bytes the bus can move each second at most.
analogy: how many trolleys per minute the corridor can take, times their load.
precise: peak bandwidth = width in bytes × transfers per second; the sustained rate is lower because of arbitration, address phases, wait states and protocol overhead.
source: D2, W1 of F1-40 (pending verification; D2 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a small storage place inside a device that software reads or writes to control it or to ask its state.
analogy: a hatch or a little window in the corridor wall.
precise: a location in a device, with a fixed width and documented bit fields, accessed by the CPU through bus transactions; reads and writes may have side effects (F1-40 showed how the address reaches the device).
source: D1 of F1-41 (pending verification; D1 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: device registers placed in the same address space as memory, used with ordinary load and store instructions.
analogy: hatches that look like pantry shelves.
precise: an I/O method in which device registers occupy physical address ranges of the memory address space, so the CPU's normal load/store instructions access them; the address decoder routes those addresses to the device.
source: D1, D2 of F1-41 (pending verification; D1/D2 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: on x86 PCs, a second, separate set of addresses only for devices, used with special instructions.
analogy: the intercom panel with its own button numbers.
precise: an x86 I/O address space separate from memory, accessed only by the in and out instruction family; the CPU controls which privilege levels may use them.
source: D4, R4 of F1-41 (pending verification; D4 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: something that happens in the device because you read or wrote a register.
analogy: taking the tray from the window turns the light off.
precise: a state change caused by the access itself, for example reading a receive-data register removing the byte from the device's buffer, or writing 1 to a status bit clearing it.
source: D1, D7 of F1-41 (pending verification; D1/D7 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a status bit you clear by writing a 1 to it.
analogy: pressing the "seen it" button next to the light.
precise: a register-bit convention in which writing 1 clears the bit and writing 0 leaves it unchanged, so software can acknowledge one event without disturbing others.
source: C1 of F1-41 (pending verification)

simple: read the register, change only your bits, write it back.
analogy: moving only your own jar on a shared shelf.
precise: an update sequence that preserves bits the software does not own (including reserved bits whose value must be preserved); it is not atomic unless the hardware or a lock makes it so.
source: C1 of F1-41 (pending verification)

simple: a C++ word that tells the compiler "this value can change behind your back; really read and write it every time".
analogy: the rule "look again each time" for the hatch windows.
precise: a type qualifier; accesses through a volatile glvalue are observable behaviour, so the compiler must perform each one, in program order relative to other volatile accesses; it does not make accesses atomic and is not a CPU memory barrier.
source: D5, R2 of F1-41 (pending verification; D5 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one complete numbering of places that addresses can name.
analogy: one set of shelf numbers; the intercom panel has its own set.
precise: a range of addresses with its own decoding; an x86 PC has (at least) a memory address space and a separate I/O port address space, which QEMU's info mtree prints separately.
source: Q1, R5 of F1-41 (pending verification)

simple: the program asks the device again and again "anything for me?".
analogy: walking to the back door every few minutes.
precise: software repeatedly reads a device status register and acts when a condition is true; simple and predictable, but it costs CPU time when nothing happens and reacts no faster than the polling period.
source: D2 of F1-42 (pending verification; D2 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a signal from a device that makes the CPU stop what it is doing for a moment, run a special function, and then continue.
analogy: the doorbell.
precise: an asynchronous event, raised by hardware outside the instruction stream, that causes the processor to finish or abandon the current instruction, save enough state to resume, and transfer control to a handler; after the handler, the interrupted code resumes.
source: D3, D2 of F1-42 (pending verification; D3/D2 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the device's "please ring" signal.
analogy: the courier pressing the bell button.
precise: the signal (a wire level or edge, or a message on newer buses) that a device uses to request an interrupt; "IRQ number" also names the input line or interrupt number in an operating system.
source: D2, R3 of F1-42 (pending verification; D2 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the small function that runs when the doorbell rings.
analogy: taking the box, saying "got it", going back to the pan.
precise: an interrupt service routine: code entered through the CPU's vector mechanism for one interrupt; it services the device (reads data, acknowledges the cause) and returns with a special return sequence that restores the interrupted state.
source: D3, D4 of F1-42 (pending verification; D3/D4 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the number that says which handler to run.
analogy: the bell's room number on the panel in the kitchen.
precise: an index into a table of handler addresses (on x86 the IDT, on Cortex-M the vector table); the CPU reads the entry for the vector and jumps to it.
source: D4, D5 of F1-42 (pending verification; D4/D5 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: telling the device (and the controller) "I have seen it".
analogy: saying "got it" so the courier stops ringing.
precise: the handler's actions that remove the cause in the device (for example reading the data register, or writing a W1C status bit, F1-41) and signal end-of-interrupt to the interrupt controller (F1-43).
source: D2 of F1-42 (pending verification; D2 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a new byte arrived before software took the previous one, so a byte was lost.
analogy: the box knocked off the step into the rain.
precise: a receiver error: a received character could not be stored because the holding register or FIFO was full; UARTs report it in a status bit (the Linux header names the 16550's UART_LSR_OE).
source: D6, L1 of F1-42 (pending verification; D6 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a fixed row of slots used in a circle: the writer adds at the head, the reader takes from the tail.
analogy: the shelf beside the door.
precise: a circular FIFO queue in an array with head and tail indices that wrap modulo its size; with one producer (the handler) and one consumer (the main program) it decouples arrival from processing.
source: D8, R2 of F1-42 (pending verification; D8 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how long it takes from the doorbell ringing to the handler starting.
analogy: finishing the stir before walking to the door.
precise: the time from the assertion of an interrupt request to the first instruction of its handler; it grows when interrupts are masked or a higher-priority handler is running.
source: D2 of F1-42 (pending verification; D2 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the part that collects the interrupt requests of many devices and passes them to the CPU one at a time, most urgent first.
analogy: the panel of bell lights by the pass.
precise: a hardware block between devices and processors that latches requests, applies per-source masks and priorities, selects the target CPU, delivers an interrupt with a vector or identifier, and tracks active interrupts until software signals completion.
source: D2, C1 of F1-43 (pending verification; D2 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: three states of a request: waiting, silenced, being handled.
analogy: the bell's light is on; its switch is off; the chef is at that door now.
precise: a request is pending after the source asserts it and before the CPU accepts it (the classic PC controller calls this register IRR); masked when software disabled the source (IMR); in service after acceptance and before end-of-interrupt (ISR).
source: D6, R3 of F1-43 (pending verification; D6 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the handler's "I am done" message to the controller.
analogy: pressing "done" on the panel.
precise: a write by software to the controller (a command register, or the GIC's end-of-interrupt register, or the PLIC's claim/complete register) that ends the in-service state, so the controller may deliver that source and lower-priority ones again.
source: D2, C1 of F1-43 (pending verification; D2 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: edge: "a ring happened"; level: "someone is still at the door".
analogy: a bell that rings once when pressed, versus a light that stays on while a visitor waits.
precise: an edge-triggered input records a transition of the request signal; a level-triggered input sees the request as long as the signal is asserted, so the source must be cleared before EOI or the interrupt is delivered again.
source: D2 of F1-43 (pending verification; D2 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: instead of a wire, the device sends a small memory write that means "interrupt".
analogy: a note pushed through a slot in the panel instead of a bell wire.
precise: an interrupt delivered as a memory write of a programmed data value to a programmed address that the interrupt controller decodes; PCI devices announce MSI and MSI-X in their capability lists.
source: D7, L1 of F1-43 (pending verification; D7 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the x86 interrupt controllers of today: one I/O APIC collects device lines; each CPU core has its own local APIC.
analogy: a panel per floor (I/O APIC) and a pager on each chef's belt (local APIC).
precise: the Advanced Programmable Interrupt Controller architecture: an I/O APIC with a redirection table entry per input pin (vector, destination, trigger mode, mask), and a local APIC per logical CPU that accepts interrupts, holds in-service state and receives EOI.
source: D4, D5, R3 of F1-43 (pending verification; D4/D5 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the standard interrupt controller of Arm application processors.
analogy: the same panel, built by a different firm.
precise: the Arm Generic Interrupt Controller; in version 3 a distributor, one redistributor per CPU, CPU interfaces, and an optional ITS that turns device messages into interrupts.
source: D8, R5 of F1-43 (pending verification; D8 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: RISC-V's controller for device interrupts, and its block for timer and software interrupts.
analogy: the panel, and a separate kitchen timer and intercom per chef.
precise: the Platform-Level Interrupt Controller routes external interrupts with priorities and per-context claim/complete; the ACLINT provides machine-level timer (MTIMER) and software (MSWI/SSWI) interrupts per hart.
source: D9, R4 of F1-43 (pending verification; D9 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a device copies data to or from memory by itself, while the CPU does other work.
analogy: the delivery truck that unloads straight into the pantry.
precise: a transfer in which a device (or a DMA engine) acts as bus master and issues memory reads or writes without the CPU executing a load or store per item; the CPU sets up the transfer and is told of completion, usually by an interrupt.
source: D2, R1 of F1-44 (pending verification; D2 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the CPU moves every piece of data itself with its own loads and stores.
analogy: the chef carrying each crate.
precise: data transfer in which the processor executes an instruction for every unit moved between a device register and memory.
source: D2 of F1-44 (pending verification; D2 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a small record in memory that tells the device what to copy, from where, to where, how much.
analogy: the delivery note.
precise: a data structure in memory, in a format defined by the device, holding at least a buffer address and a length plus control and status bits; the device reads descriptors and writes back status.
source: D7, R1 of F1-44 (pending verification; D7 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a circular list of descriptors shared by the driver and the device.
analogy: a clipboard of delivery notes that goes round and round.
precise: a ring buffer of descriptors in memory with a producer index and a consumer index, one owned by the driver and one by the device; the driver tells the device about new entries by writing a "doorbell" register.
source: D7 of F1-44 (pending verification; D7 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one transfer made of several pieces of memory in different places.
analogy: one delivery note listing several shelves.
precise: DMA driven by a list of (address, length) pairs, so a buffer need not be contiguous in physical memory.
source: D7 of F1-44 (pending verification; D7 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: making sure the CPU's cached copy and memory agree when a device reads or writes memory.
analogy: the chef's worktable and the pantry shelf holding the same vegetables.
precise: a system is DMA-coherent if device accesses to memory see the latest CPU writes in caches and invalidate or update cached copies; on a non-coherent system software must clean (write back) and invalidate cache lines around each transfer.
source: D2, R2 of F1-44 (pending verification; D2 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: clean: copy changed cached data to memory; invalidate: throw the cached copy away so the next read goes to memory.
analogy: putting worktable vegetables back on the shelf; clearing the worktable.
precise: cache maintenance operations on a range of addresses: clean writes dirty lines back to memory; invalidate marks lines not valid.
source: D2, R2 of F1-44 (pending verification; D2 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a translator and guard between devices and memory: devices use their own addresses, and may only reach memory they were given.
analogy: the gatekeeper at the loading bay, with a list of shelves each truck may use.
precise: an input–output memory management unit that translates device-issued addresses (I/O virtual addresses) to physical addresses through per-device page tables and blocks accesses without a mapping; many also remap interrupts.
source: D8, R4, C1 of F1-44 (pending verification; D8 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a spare buffer the device can reach, used when it cannot reach the real one; data is copied between them.
analogy: a trolley at the gate when the truck may not enter the building.
precise: a buffer in device-addressable memory used for DMA when the real buffer is outside the device's address range or not suitable, at the cost of a CPU copy.
source: D9 of F1-44 (pending verification; D9 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the main expansion bus of PCs and servers: fast serial links between the processor and cards such as GPUs, network cards and drives.
analogy: the food hall's corridors, one private corridor per stall.
precise: a point-to-point, packet-based serial interconnect that keeps the software model of PCI (configuration space, BARs, memory and I/O transactions) while carrying them as transaction-layer packets over one or more lanes per link.
source: D3, C1 of F1-45 (pending verification; D3 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the three-part address of one PCI device or part of a device.
analogy: floor, stall, counter.
precise: a PCI function is addressed by its bus number, device number on that bus and function number within the device, written for example 00:1f.2; one physical device can have several functions.
source: D3, R1 of F1-45 (pending verification; D3 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a small block of registers every PCI function has, describing what it is and how to set it up.
analogy: the standard card at the stall door.
precise: a per-function register space, separate from memory and I/O space, with a standard 64-byte header (identification, command, status, class code, base address registers, capability pointer) followed by capability structures; 256 bytes in PCI and 4096 bytes in PCI Express.
source: L1, D3 of F1-45 (pending verification; D3 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a register in which software tells the device where in the address map its registers or memory should appear.
analogy: the space on the card where the manager writes "rooms 400 to 403".
precise: a configuration register that describes a memory or I/O window the function decodes: its low bits say the type (I/O or memory, 32- or 64-bit, prefetchable) and are read-only; software discovers the size by writing all ones and reading back, then programs the base address.
source: L1, R4 of F1-45 (pending verification)

simple: the start-up walk that finds every PCI device and gives each its addresses.
analogy: the manager's morning walk.
precise: the process (in firmware, the OS or both) of probing each bus, device and function for a valid vendor ID, numbering the buses behind bridges, sizing and assigning BARs, and enabling decoding and bus mastering in the command register.
source: D3, C1 of F1-45 (pending verification; D3 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a chain of optional feature blocks in configuration space.
analogy: extra pages stapled to the card, each pointing to the next.
precise: a linked list starting at the offset in the capability pointer register (0x34), each entry beginning with an ID byte and a next-pointer byte; IDs include power management, MSI, MSI-X, PCI Express and vendor-specific.
source: L1, R2 of F1-45 (pending verification)
related: Root complex, root port, switch, endpoint

term: Root complex, root port, switch, endpoint
simple: the parts of the PCIe tree: the processor's side, its sockets, branching boxes, and the devices at the ends.
analogy: the building's core, its corridor exits, junctions, and the stalls.
precise: the root complex connects the CPU and memory to the PCIe hierarchy through root ports; a switch fans one upstream link out to several downstream ports (each appearing to software as a PCI-to-PCI bridge); endpoints are the devices that issue and receive transactions.
source: D3, R1 of F1-45 (pending verification; D3 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a link is a connection between two PCIe ports; it has 1 or more lanes (pairs of wires each way); data travels in packets.
analogy: a corridor, its number of walking lanes, and the parcels carried.
precise: a PCIe link aggregates lanes, each a differential pair in each direction; reads, writes, completions and messages travel as transaction-layer packets (TLPs), protected and retried by the data-link layer.
source: D3, D5 of F1-45 (pending verification; D3/D5 title only, dossier gate G1 open)
related: Root complex, root port, switch, endpoint

simple: the computer side of USB, which runs the bus and asks every device in turn.
analogy: the waiter and the waiter's station.
precise: the host schedules all transfers on a USB bus; the host controller (for example xHCI, a PCI device, F1-45) carries out the schedule and contains the root hub with the first ports.
source: D1, R1 of F1-46 (pending verification; D1 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a box that turns one USB port into several.
analogy: a side table where several gadgets sit together.
precise: a USB device class that repeats traffic between an upstream port and several downstream ports and reports attach and detach events; devices behind it get port paths such as 2.1.
source: D1, R1 of F1-46 (pending verification; D1 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one numbered "mailbox" inside a device, for data in one direction.
analogy: the in-tray and out-tray on a gadget.
precise: an addressable source or sink of data in a device, identified by number and direction (IN = device to host, OUT = host to device); endpoint 0 is the bidirectional control endpoint every device has.
source: D1, L1 of F1-46 (pending verification; D1 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: four ways to move data: control (setup questions), bulk (lots of data, whenever there is time), interrupt (small, regular checks), isochronous (steady streams like audio).
analogy: forms at check-in, parcels, a regular "anything for me?", a conveyor belt.
precise: control transfers carry a SETUP stage, optional data and a status stage; bulk transfers use spare bandwidth with error retry; interrupt transfers are polled at a bounded interval; isochronous transfers get reserved bandwidth without retry (USB_ENDPOINT_XFER_CONTROL 0, ISOC 1, BULK 2, INT 3 in ch9.h).
source: L1, D1 of F1-46 (pending verification; D1 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a small record a device sends to describe itself.
analogy: the gadget's ID card.
precise: a byte structure beginning with its length and type: the device descriptor (type 1), configuration (2), interface (4), endpoint (5), and class-specific descriptors; the host reads them with GET_DESCRIPTOR requests.
source: L1, R3 of F1-46 (pending verification)

simple: what happens when you plug a device in: the host gives it an address, reads its descriptors and switches it on.
analogy: the standard questions at check-in.
precise: the host detects attachment on a port, resets it, assigns a device address, reads the device and configuration descriptors, selects a configuration (SET_CONFIGURATION) and loads a class or vendor driver.
source: D1, R2 of F1-46 (pending verification; D1 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a standard type of device, so one driver can serve devices from many makers.
analogy: "all keyboards answer the same questions the same way".
precise: a class code in the device or interface descriptor (for example 3 = HID, human interface device, USB_CLASS_HID) with a class specification defining requests, descriptors and data formats.
source: L1, D2 of F1-46 (pending verification; D2 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the 8-byte question that starts a control transfer.
analogy: the form the waiter hands over.
precise: eight bytes: bmRequestType (direction, type, recipient), bRequest, wValue, wIndex, wLength (the number of data bytes the host wants); the Linux header defines it as struct usb_ctrlrequest.
source: L1, R3 of F1-46 (pending verification)

simple: a two-wire bus where one controller talks to many small chips, each with its own address.
analogy: the shared speaking tube where you call a name.
precise: a synchronous, half-duplex serial bus with a clock line (SCL) and a data line (SDA), both open-drain with pull-up resistors; transfers start with a START condition and a 7-bit (or 10-bit) address plus a read/write bit, each byte is followed by an acknowledge bit, and a STOP condition ends the transfer.
source: D1, L2 of F1-47 (pending verification; D1 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: every chip can only pull the wire low or let go; a resistor pulls it high when everyone lets go.
analogy: a rope that anyone can pull down, held up by a spring.
precise: an output that either sinks current or is high-impedance; with a pull-up the line is low if any device pulls it low, so the line is the logical AND of all outputs and no two drivers can fight.
source: D1, R1 of F1-47 (pending verification; D1 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the receiver's "got it" (pull SDA low) or silence (leave it high) after every byte.
analogy: a grunt down the tube after each word.
precise: the ninth clock of each I2C byte, during which the receiver pulls SDA low to acknowledge; a high level (NACK) means no device answered the address, the receiver refused the byte, or the controller signals the last byte of a read.
source: D1, R1 of F1-47 (pending verification; D1 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a fast four-wire link where the controller picks one chip with its own select wire and swaps bits with it.
analogy: private string telephones, one cord per scale.
precise: a synchronous, full-duplex serial interface with a clock (SCLK), controller-out data (MOSI, also COPI), controller-in data (MISO, CIPO) and one chip-select line per target; each clock shifts one bit each way, so a transfer exchanges the contents of two shift registers; clock polarity and phase (the "SPI mode") must match.
source: D2, R3 of F1-47 (pending verification; D2 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a serial line with no clock wire: both sides agree on the speed in advance.
analogy: the line to the bar, where both agreed how fast to talk.
precise: a universal asynchronous receiver-transmitter sends frames of a start bit (low), 5–8 data bits least significant first, an optional parity bit and 1 or 2 stop bits (high) at a configured baud rate; the receiver resynchronises on each start bit and samples in the middle of each bit.
source: D3, L1, R2 of F1-47 (pending verification; D3 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how many signal changes (here, bits) per second the line uses.
analogy: the agreed talking speed.
precise: symbols per second; for a two-level UART line, one symbol is one bit, so 9600 baud is 9600 bit times per second including start and stop bits; both ends derive it from their own clocks with a divisor.
source: D3, L1 of F1-47 (pending verification; D3 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a robust two-wire bus for cars and machines, where every message has an ID and the lowest ID wins when two talk at once.
analogy: the van's shared wire where the most urgent message goes first.
precise: the Controller Area Network: a multi-controller, message-based differential bus with dominant (0) and recessive (1) levels; frames carry an 11-bit or 29-bit identifier, up to 8 data bytes (64 in CAN FD) and a CRC; bitwise arbitration on the identifier resolves collisions without destroying the winning frame.
source: D4, L3, R4 of F1-47 (pending verification; D4 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a tool that records many digital wires over time and can decode protocols from the recording.
analogy: a recorder on every speaking tube.
precise: an instrument that samples digital signals at a fixed rate, stores the samples, and displays them as waveforms; protocol decoders (for example in sigrok's PulseView) turn the samples into START, addresses, bytes and ACKs.
source: D5 of F1-47 (pending verification; D5 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the part that makes a steady tick; a quartz crystal makes it very steady.
analogy: the pendulum of the kitchen clock.
precise: an oscillator is a circuit that produces a periodic signal; a quartz crystal resonator sets its frequency precisely, while an RC oscillator is cheaper and less accurate; the frequency's deviation is usually given in parts per million (ppm).
source: D1, D2 of F1-48 (pending verification; D1/D2 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a PLL makes a faster clock from a slower one; a divider makes a slower one.
analogy: gears between the pendulum and the hands.
precise: a phase-locked loop multiplies a reference frequency by a ratio by locking a controlled oscillator's divided output to the reference; dividers and prescalers divide a clock by an integer; together they produce the clocks of the CPU, buses and peripherals (the clock tree).
source: D1 of F1-48 (pending verification; D1 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a counter driven by a clock that raises an interrupt when it reaches a set value.
analogy: the oven timer.
precise: a peripheral with a counter register clocked from a (prescaled) clock, a reload or compare register, and status and interrupt-enable bits; on reaching the compare value or overflowing it sets a flag, raises an interrupt and may reload.
source: D2, R1 of F1-48 (pending verification; D2 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the prescaler slows the counter's clock; the reload value sets how far it counts before it rings.
analogy: choosing "count every eighth tick" and "ring after 2000 counts".
precise: the prescaler divides the input clock; for a counter that counts 0 … reload and wraps, the period is (reload + 1) × prescaler / fin.
source: R1, W1 of F1-48 (pending verification)
related: Input capture, output compare and PWM

term: Input capture, output compare and PWM
simple: capture writes down the time of an outside event; compare does something at a set time; PWM makes a square wave whose high part you choose.
analogy: a stopwatch button; an alarm; a light switched on for part of every second.
precise: input capture copies the counter into a register on a pin edge; output compare sets, clears or toggles a pin or raises an interrupt when the counter equals a register; pulse-width modulation uses a period and a compare value to produce a duty cycle.
source: D2 of F1-48 (pending verification; D2 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a timer that resets the computer unless the program "pats" it in time.
analogy: a dead man's switch.
precise: an independent counter that triggers a reset (or an interrupt first) on expiry; correct software restarts it periodically, so a hung program causes a reset.
source: D2 of F1-48 (pending verification; D2 title only, dossier gate G1 open)
related: Input capture, output compare and PWM

simple: a counter that reaches its biggest value goes back to zero.
analogy: a clock face going from 12 back to 1.
precise: an n-bit counter counts modulo 2n; time comparisons must use modular differences, not plain "greater than".
source: R2, D3 of F1-48 (pending verification; D3 title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the hardware counter the operating system reads to tell the time.
analogy: the one clock on the wall everybody trusts.
precise: a free-running counter with known frequency (on x86, for example the TSC or HPET; in a virtual machine, a paravirtual clock) that the kernel reads to keep time; Linux lists the candidates and the current one in sysfs.
source: R4, C1 of F1-48 (pending verification)
